posts.title: Why We Still Chart Qualitative Interviews on Paper Walls
posts.excerpt: In an industry increasingly governed by automated analytics, Shirabe Research relies on physical paper charts and in-person interviews to uncover what customers truly mean.
posts.content:
Every Monday morning at Shirabe Research begins with the same deliberate ritual. In our studio on the fourth floor of 27 Calder Street in Northbank, long sheets of heavy butcher paper are pinned across the walls of Studio B. Before a single customer sits down across our table, the room is quiet, uncluttered, and stripped of digital distraction. For over twelve years since our founding in 2012, our seven-person practice has resisted the prevailing trend toward automated customer telemetry, sentiment algorithms, and synthetic research personas. We believe that understanding human intent requires physical presence, unhurried attention, and the tactile discipline of paper.

The modern product organization is awash in quantitative data. Analytics dashboards register click frequencies, drop-off rates, and session durations down to the millisecond. Yet when customer engagement falters, numbers alone cannot explain the underlying reason. In our recent work with grocery co-op members investigating why app engagement had dropped, digital dashboards showed only that screens were being closed within seconds. It was only when our moderators sat across the table from members in our interview studio that the reality emerged. Shoppers were standing in store aisles where concrete walls blocked connectivity, holding printed weekly circulars because they trusted physical paper over an unreliable barcode scanner.

This gap between digital assumption and physical reality is why our method centers on small, rigorous samples. A typical Shirabe Research study spans five weeks and examines eight to twelve deeply screened participants. We do not use anonymous mass panels. Instead, recruitment lead Ingrid Solberg verifies each participant against actual behavioral habits, ensuring that every sixty-minute session in Studio A or Studio B yields authentic testimony. Senior moderators Clara Wendt and Nadia Haddad guide these conversations without scripted checklists, allowing participants the breathing room to hesitate, correct themselves, and voice the subtle frustrations they normally conceal from digital surveys.

Once fieldwork concludes, our team does not feed transcripts into automated summarization software. Instead, Wei-Lin Chou prepares verbatim transcripts, and our researchers gather in the studio to chart findings directly by hand. We write participant quotes onto paper cards, tack them to the wall charts, and organize them into visual clusters alongside head of fieldwork Tomás Ibarra and analysis lead Jonah Mensah. When client teams join us for week four of the study, they do not stare at slide decks. They walk the perimeter of the room, inspect raw quotations, and trace how six or nine clear findings were assembled from primary evidence.

Physical paper enforces an honesty that digital presentations easily obscure. You cannot bury an uncomfortable participant contradiction when it is pinned to the wall at eye level in black ink. Charting on paper demands debate, collective inspection, and tactile synthesis. By the time we deliver our final readout in week five, every stakeholder understands not merely what was concluded, but how each conclusion was built from real voices. In an era eager to automate human conversation, sitting across the table and writing on paper remains the most dependable path to genuine customer truth.
